source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models
finding: Codex and PaLM few-shot translate MATH problems into Isabelle. Human check of Codex outputs: only a quarter perfect; most failures are concept misalignment.
numbers: 150 random MATH problems (50 algebra, 50 number theory, 50 intermediate algebra); 38 perfect = 25.3%. Perfect by subject: 13, 17, 8.
limits: Small human-checked sample, one model, Isabelle only. Prompts were hand-written per subject. Example failure: 'the greatest possible value' not mapped to Max.
agent_relevance: Statement translation is brittle on definition alignment; an agent must check the formal statement against the text, not trust one pass.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models (failure table)
finding: Failure modes by subject for Codex formalisations.
numbers: Fail to align definitions: 10 algebra, 18 number theory, 18 intermediate algebra. Wrong function use: 6, 13, 16. Missing Isabelle definition: 0, 12, 3. Syntax/type error: 7, 2, 11. Inconsistent/missing assumption: 8, 9, 9. Unclear prompt: 9, 3, 14.
limits: N is 50 per subject; categories may overlap.
agent_relevance: Most errors are semantic (alignment, missing assumptions), not syntax. Compiler feedback alone cannot catch them.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models (BLEU and scaling)
finding: On miniF2F (140 algebra, 120 number theory), BLEU of PaLM translations rises steadily from 8B to 540B. Codex beats PaLM on BLEU, likely because it saw more formal data.
numbers: PaLM 8B to 540B: monotone BLEU gain in both subjects (exact table not copied).
limits: BLEU is a weak proxy for correctness (see later work).
agent_relevance: Larger or code-trained models help, but BLEU gains need a semantic check.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models (use for proving)
finding: Autoformalised statements were used as extra training data for expert iteration on a prover.
numbers: miniF2F proof rate raised from 29.6% to 35.2% (state of the art then).
limits: The gain comes from using formalised MATH statements as training problems, not from each being exact.
agent_relevance: Autoformalised problems can bootstrap a solver even when only some are exact.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Draft, Sketch, and Prove
finding: LLM writes an informal proof, maps it to a formal sketch with gaps, an automated prover fills the gaps. Autoformalising the proof sketch lifts proof rates.
numbers: miniF2F-test: 20.9% (Sledgehammer+heuristics baseline) to 39.3% with human informal proofs; Minerva 62B informal proofs 37.7% test, 43.9% valid.
limits: Only 58% of 50 sampled model informal proofs were correct, yet sketches still worked.
agent_relevance: A draft, formalise, verify loop is a working scaffold pattern.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Draft, Sketch, and Prove (ablations)
finding: Ablations show what matters in sketch formalisation.
numbers: Without in-line comments: -4.9 (valid) and -2.8 (test) points. Using model instead of human informal proof: roughly -3.7 and -5.3 points. Without automated prover closing gaps: -9.8 and -9.0 points.
limits: Table text partly garbled in extraction; drops only are reported.
agent_relevance: The external prover that closes gaps is worth the most (about 9 points); informal draft helps less than formal tooling.

finding: Benchmark of 371 undergraduate theorem statements in Lean 3 with NL statements. Few-shot Codex gets 13.4% exact formalisation.
numbers: Few-shot Codex: typecheck 23.7%, BLEU 25.1, accuracy 13.4%. proofGPT-1.3B/6.7B few-shot: accuracy 0.
limits: Lean 3 only; later work found 31.8% of Lean 4 port entries had errors.
agent_relevance: Baseline for how weak plain prompting is on undergraduate maths.

source: Azerbayev et al. (2023) ProofNet (retrieval and distillation)
finding: Prompt retrieval of related Mathlib items and distilled backtranslation change results.
numbers: Prompt retrieval Codex: typecheck 45.2%, BLEU 14.8, accuracy 16.1%. Distilled backtranslation proofGPT-1.3B: typecheck 19.4%, accuracy 3.2%.
limits: Retrieval roughly doubled typecheck rate but accuracy rose only 2.7 points. Table layout was garbled; row mapping inferred.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of definitions fixes syntax and naming first; semantic faithfulness lags.

finding: Going formal to informal is much easier than the reverse for Codex.
numbers: Informalisation accuracy 62.3% vs formalisation 13.4% (371 statements).
quote: among generations that typecheck, roughly half are correct
limits: Informalisation judged by humans.
agent_relevance: Back-translation is a cheap but imperfect check; model understands formal maths better than it writes it.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Multilingual Mathematical Autoformalization (MMA)
finding: Large dataset made by informalising formal statements with an LLM, then fine-tuning for the forward direction.
numbers: Fine-tuned models: 16-18% of statements acceptable with minimal corrections on miniF2F and ProofNet (50 outputs each), up from 0% for base. Joint Isabelle+Lean4 training beat monolingual.
limits: Small human-checked samples (50). Compile rate and acceptance differ greatly.
agent_relevance: Synthetic backtranslation data helps, and training on several formal languages transfers.

finding: Iterative pipeline: formalise, compile, backtranslate, NLI check, human diagnosis, retrain. Six rounds.
numbers: About 57K formal-informal pairs; sampled human accuracy 93.5% (weighted over problem tags); stopped when sampled correct rate near 95%; Pass@1024 of provers 8.6% on the hard set.
limits: Accuracy is on sampled pairs judged by experts; filters leave out hard problems.
agent_relevance: Layered filters (compile, back-translate, NLI, human) are a template for checking an agent's own formalisations.

finding: Uses Lean 4 compiler feedback as a process signal for autoformalisation, with a benchmark FormL4.
numbers: Enhanced autoformalizer: Basic test greedy 35.67, pass@1 33.14, pass@5 43.11; Random 27.43/26.47/36.19; Real 23.72/22.29/40.33 (row mapping from garbled table). GPT-4 real-test greedy 10.20% vs best open-source 1.10%.
limits: Row labels were ambiguous in extracted text.
agent_relevance: Compiler feedback during training helps; real textbook text is much harder than synthetic.

source: Poiroux et al. (2024) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization
finding: Proposes BEq+ metric and finds 31.8% of ProofNet Lean 4 entries were wrong; builds corrected ProofNet#.
numbers: ProofNetVerif: 3,752 human-labelled pairs. ProofNet# accuracy 31.0% (single sample) to 45.1% (50 samples plus type-check filter plus selection).
limits: BEq+ is an approximation; accuracy of metric varies by statement length.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks themselves carry errors; older reported scores are partly unreliable.

finding: Sampling many formalisations, keeping only those that type-check, then picking by Self-BLEU or majority vote gives large gains.
numbers: Llemma 7B BEq+ pass@n: 4.11% at n=1, 40.54% at n=1000. Gains of +8.7 to +18.4 points over greedy. Symbolic-equivalence selection no better than Self-BLEU or majority vote.
limits: Pass@n is an upper bound; real selection recovers only part of it.
agent_relevance: Cheap scaffold: sample, compile-check, then self-consistency. Do the type-check filter first.

finding: On 619 research-level pairs without in-file context, all models are near zero; context is the missing piece.
numbers: Table 4 RLM25 no context: BEq+ about 0.4-2.8% across Llama3 8B, Llemma 7B, GPT-4o (1.50%). BEq+ metric agreement with humans drops from 62.5% on short to 29.6% on long statements (as read from text).
limits: Without local definitions and namespaces, the task is under-specified.
agent_relevance: Give the agent project context (definitions, notation); a bare sentence is not enough.

source: Murphy et al. (2024) Autoformalizing Euclidean Geometry
finding: LeanEuclid benchmark; GPT-4 and GPT-4V with few-shot prompts. Theorem prover fills diagram gaps; SMT checks semantic equivalence.
numbers: Theorem statements: GPT-4 18.9%, GPT-4V 21.0% correct. Proofs: GPT-4 18.8% vs GPT-4V 23.1% on LeanEuclid. Checker false-negative rate about 15.8%.
limits: Vision helps only slightly; formal system E is poor as a specification language.
agent_relevance: Domain tools (SMT) can give automatic semantic checks where equivalence is decidable.

finding: 5,560 Lean 4 problems built by human-in-the-loop autoformalisation with multi-LLM semantic check and negation filtering.
numbers: Pipeline keeps 72.09% before manual check; best prover only 16.46% under sampling budget; semantic voting cut 92.4% compile-passing statements to 32.7% (60.7% filtered); 21.7% of candidates finally formalised.
limits: Semantic checkers are other LLMs, so shared blind spots are possible. Agreement much lower on undergraduate level (4.63% on HardMath).
agent_relevance: Compile success is a poor guide to faithfulness; a multi-judge vote removes most false positives.

source: Yu et al. (2025) FormalMATH (negation and NL guidance)
finding: Negation-based disproof filtering removed a small share of false or unprovable statements. Natural-language solution guidance was linked to worse proof success.
numbers: Negation filter removed 1.6% of statements.
quote: counterintuitive inverse relationship between natural-language solution guidance and proof success
limits: Main filter is the semantic vote, not negation.
agent_relevance: Trying to prove the negation is a cheap sanity check; human-written informal reasoning may add noise.

finding: Translator fine-tuned on Mathlib4 with informal annotations from Lean analysis, plus retrieval.
numbers: miniF2F-test Pass@128: 93.2% vs InternLM2-Math-Plus-7B 74.0% and TheoremLlama 50.1%. Graduate-level textbook set: 22.5% vs 7.5% and 4.0%.
limits: Compile-type accuracy on miniF2F is near ceiling; textbook-level still low.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks like miniF2F are saturated; harder sources are needed.

finding: Two formalisers trained to convert Numina problems to Lean 4, giving 1.64M statements used to train a prover.
numbers: Formalizer B (trained on 170K of 230K Claude-formalised statements that compiled): CC Pass@1 88.48% vs A 76.74%; FC (faithfulness) Pass@1 80.42% vs 48.06%; CC+FC Pass@1 76.41% vs 45.72%. Pass@8 CC+FC 95.78% vs 82.33%.
limits: Faithfulness is judged by Qwen2.5-72B, not humans.
agent_relevance: Formalisation style changes prover results; model-judged faithfulness is the scalable check.

finding: Mixing statements from both formalisers beats either alone; ProofNet moves opposite to miniF2F.
numbers: miniF2F 57.6% mixed vs 56.5%/56.2% single; ProofNet 15.2% vs 13.8%/15.2%. Mathlib4 data helps ProofNet but hurts miniF2F.
limits: Differences of 1 to 2 points, single runs.
agent_relevance: Diverse formalisations of one problem add robustness; distribution shift between olympiad and textbook maths is real.

finding: Data-generation loop (concept repository, expert iteration, distillation, augmentation) trains a Llama3.1-8B translator.
numbers: 117k statements; MathQual pass@1/8/32: 22.75/45.85/58.23% vs Kimina-Autoformalizer 19.01/38.97/50.71% and Herald 10.92/31.83/45.33%. ProofNet pass@1 39.46% vs Herald 31.43%. Significant at p<0.05 except ProofNet pass@32.
limits: Compilation pass rate, not full semantic check, in main table.
agent_relevance: Small 8B models can match big ones when data is built iteratively.

finding: Trained scorer for alignment of formal and informal statements; reduces manual checking.
numbers: Alignment-Selection score 99.21% vs GPT-4 88.91% on FormL4-Basic; 66.39% vs 64.34% on miniF2F-Valid.
limits: Tested on synthetically built misalignments; real error distribution may differ.
agent_relevance: A learned alignment score can rank candidate formalisations.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Don't Trust: Verify (DTV)
finding: Autoformalise each informal solution in Isabelle and keep only self-consistent ones; beats majority vote.
numbers: Minerva 62B solve rates: single sample 42.8% avg; majority vote 61.5%; DTV 65.0%; DTV with GPT-3.5 formalising 68.2%. GSM8K 79.4% vs 67.2% majority (+12.2 pts). Row mapping read from garbled table.
limits: Relies on a decent formaliser; mostly grade-school and algebra.
agent_relevance: Autoformalisation used inside an answer-filtering loop; fits a verify step.

finding: LLM translates logic problems to symbolic form; a solver reasons.
numbers: Avg +39.2% over standard prompting and +18.4% over CoT (GPT-3.5). GPT-4 Logic-LM: ProofWriter 79.66, FOLIO 78.92, LogicalDeduction 87.63, AR-LSAT 43.04; but PrOntoQA 83.20 below CoT 98.79.
limits: On PrOntoQA CoT wins; AR-LSAT executable rate only 32.6% (GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Translation to logic helps most on non-linear tasks; hurts on simple forward chains.

finding: Solver error messages feed back to repair the formalisation.
numbers: GPT-4 FOLIO executable rate 79.9% to 85.8%; AR-LSAT 32.6% to 39.8%; GPT-3.5 FOLIO 66.7% to 84.3%. Accuracy stagnates after the first rounds.
limits: Repairs mostly fix syntax; semantic errors remain.
agent_relevance: One or two repair rounds from tool errors; more rounds add little.

finding: LLM writes a declarative spec, SAT/SMT solver answers.
numbers: code-davinci-002 greedy: GSM-Sys 69.4 vs CoT 46.5, ProgLM 43.4; LSAT 35.0 vs 23.5; CLUTRR 68.3; ProofWriter 99.7. Without a solver accuracy is near standard prompting.
limits: Gains small on plain GSM (71.8 vs ProgLM 72.7).
agent_relevance: Declarative specs are easier to write than step plans; solver adds the guarantee.

finding: LLM as semantic parser to first-order logic plus Prover9; majority over samples.
numbers: FOLIO StarCoder+: 56.0% vs 41.8% CoT. GPT-4 on FOLIO: LINC 72.5% vs CoT 75.3%. Up to 26 points over CoT on ProofWriter (GPT-4).
limits: Not better than CoT for GPT-4 on FOLIO.
agent_relevance: Choose per task; the two methods fail differently, so combining is plausible.

finding: Failure modes of translation to FOL: lost implicit facts, mismatched predicates, syntax errors.
numbers: Syntax error rate: StarCoder+ 38%, GPT-3.5 24%, GPT-4 13%. Common cause: same symbol with different arity.
agent_relevance: Check arity and predicate consistency across premises before calling a solver.

finding: Fully LLM pipeline: translate, plan, solve with rules, verify translation and chain.
numbers: Gains over Naive/CoT/Logic-LM of 21.56/6.11/3.53 points (GPT-3.5) and 22.08/9.31/7.88 (GPT-4). Planner+Solver add about 10.4 points, Translator 6.3. Exception: FOLIO with GPT-3.5 below Logic-LM.
limits: No external prover, so errors not machine-checked.
agent_relevance: A verifier that re-checks translation is worth including; no solver needed to gain.

finding: Interactive translation of requirements to temporal logic with sub-formula back-mapping.
numbers: 36 expert instances: Codex minimal prompt 44.4%, plus in-distribution examples 58.3%, interactive 86.11% (31/36); Bloom 13.8%; fine-tuned T5 5.5%; rasa 2.7%.
limits: Only 36 instances.
agent_relevance: Human or agent edit loop on sub-translations beats whole redraft.

source: Mirchev et al. (2023) Clover: closed-loop verifiable code generation
finding: Consistency check among code, docstring and Dafny annotations.
numbers: Accepts up to 87% of correct instances (52/60 for one check), rejects 100% of adversarial wrong ones, found 6 faulty programs in MBPP-DFY-50.
limits: Textbook-level Dafny only.
agent_relevance: Cross-checking three views of one intent catches errors; no false positives in test.

finding: Tool correction and conjecture correction using prover error messages.
numbers: miniF2F valid 48.0% to 55.3%, test 45.5% to 51.2%.
limits: Isabelle proving, not statement translation.
agent_relevance: Error-message feedback loops with hard-coded repairs give measurable gains.

source: Weng et al. (2025) Autoformalization in the Era of LLMs: A Survey
finding: Survey of data, models, evaluation and use for verifying LLM outputs.
numbers: Notes formal competition problems score about 30% vs about 70% for easier informal-level tasks; lists provers at 59.8-88.9% on miniF2F.
limits: Secondary source; figures not re-checked.
agent_relevance: Use as map of 2024-25 work; main open issue is semantic evaluation.
